Chapter 10. The Endless Present: Art, Memory, and the Future.
As we step into the world of modern art today, things get a bit tricky, don’t they? It’s tough to draw sharp lines or pin down neat categories. The world’s more connected than ever... but it’s also more fragmented.
Think about it—artists now work across borders, across all sorts of media, and even across traditions. They’re just as likely to find inspiration in ancient myths as they are in the latest technology.
Picture this: In a bustling city, a young artist projects images onto the side of a building. The pictures flicker and fade, mingling with the glow of passing cars. Some people pause, drawn in for a moment. Others rush past, barely giving it a glance. And the artist? They can’t help but wonder—what will stick in people’s minds? What will be remembered, and what will simply slip away?
Meanwhile, somewhere else, there’s an older painter who keeps coming back to the same view, year after year. She paints what she sees from her window, quietly watching as the seasons change and the city itself rises and falls. It’s almost meditative—a gentle way of marking time, holding on to something steady in a world that never seems to slow down.
For so many artists, the real challenge isn’t just making something new. It’s remembering—holding on to the stories, images, and moments that give life its meaning. In a culture that’s always chasing the next big thing, the past can feel distant, maybe even disposable. But artists? They keep finding ways to honor memory, weaving together history and hope like threads in a giant tapestry.
And then, there’s the future—always just out of reach, always uncertain. Some artists dream up utopias, worlds filled with harmony and abundance. Others sound the alarm, warning us about possible disasters. But honestly, most find themselves caught somewhere in the middle—torn between hope and worry, between wanting to escape and feeling the need to engage with what’s coming.
